_comment: Site-type axis for the web-launch-readiness skill (road-to-web-launch-readiness 0.2). The design directive this file exists to enforce is CONDITIONAL, NOT FLAT: a check that applies everywhere is a check that gets ignored somewhere. Every entry declares which site types it applies to, so a SaaS app is never asked for opening hours and a docs site is never asked for a cookie banner it does not set. REGISTERED BEFORE ANY SKILL CODE EXISTS, which is the point of Phase 0: the axis is a decision, and deciding it after writing the checks would let the checks pick their own scope. Nothing reads this file yet -- the skill is gated behind b-estate-decision-web-launch.

site_types._comment: The closed enum. A check may not name a type outside it, and a type carries no checks until one lists it -- so adding a type is inert until a check opts in, and removing one is caught by the schema test rather than silently emptying a check's scope.

tiers._comment: Report order, and it is the output contract rather than a label: critical first, situational last. A finding's tier is a property of the FINDING, not of the reader's patience -- a staging noindex on a production marketing site is critical whether or not the reader has time for it.

checks.title: A staging `noindex` or `robots.txt` disallow survived into production
checks.why: The defect class with ZERO coverage in the estate (G0: `robots` 0 files, `noindex` 0 files) and the highest cost: the site ships, works, looks correct, and is invisible to search. Nothing in the tree looks for it today.
checks.remediation: Remove the `noindex` meta tag and the blanket `Disallow: /` from the production build; keep them behind the staging environment's own config rather than in shared source.
checks.verification: `curl -sI <prod-url> | grep -i x-robots-tag` returns nothing, `curl -s <prod-url>/robots.txt` carries no blanket disallow, and the rendered HTML has no `noindex` meta.

checks.title: HTTP is redirected to HTTPS and no asset is loaded over plain HTTP
checks.why: A mixed-content asset silently breaks the padlock and, on a form page, ships a credential over plaintext. Browsers block some of it and load the rest, so the page LOOKS fine while the guarantee is gone -- which is why this is critical rather than high.
checks.remediation: Serve every asset over https:// or protocol-relative paths, and redirect http:// at the edge. Never hard-code an http:// origin you control.
checks.verification: `curl -sI http://<prod-host>/` returns a 301/308 to https, and the browser console shows no mixed-content warning on the heaviest page.

checks.title: A custom 404 route exists and is reachable
checks.why: A framework default error page leaks stack shape and loses the visitor. `404` matches 19 files in the estate, all HTTP-status tables -- none is a launch check.
checks.remediation: Add the framework's custom 404 route and give it a link back into the site.
checks.verification: `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' <prod-url>/<random-path>` returns 404 and the body is the custom page, not the framework default.

checks.title: Every indexable route carries a title and a meta description
checks.why: `meta description` matches 0 files. Excluded for `saas-app` and `internal-tool` on purpose: an authenticated app's routes are not indexed, so per-route descriptions are work with no consumer.
checks.remediation: Add title and description to each route's metadata export; a shared default is a fallback, not a per-route value.
checks.verification: Fetch each route in the sitemap and assert a non-empty, non-duplicated title and description.

checks.title: Content images carry alternative text
checks.why: The one check that applies to every type, including internal tools -- an internal user with a screen reader is still a user. `alt text` matches 7 files, all accessibility prose rather than a launch check.
checks.remediation: Add `alt` to content images; decorative images take `alt=""` explicitly rather than being left without the attribute.
checks.verification: Parse the rendered HTML and assert every `` has an `alt` attribute, empty or not.

checks.title: Every page declares lang, charset and viewport
checks.why: A missing `lang` makes a screen reader guess the pronunciation of the whole page; a missing viewport makes a phone render a desktop layout at 320px. Both are one line, both are invisible on the developer's machine, and both are the kind of default a framework template silently drops when a page is hand-written.
checks.remediation: `<html lang="..">`, `<meta charset="utf-8">` and `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` in the shared layout, not per page.
checks.verification: View source on two unrelated routes and confirm all three are present on both -- one route proves the layout, two prove it is the layout and not a copy.

checks.title: Canonical URLs, sitemap and robots.txt agree with each other
checks.why: Three sources that can disagree silently: a sitemap listing a route whose canonical points elsewhere, or a robots disallow on a route the sitemap advertises. Note `canonical` matches 115 files in this estate in a completely different sense ("the canonical rule"), so its count is NOT coverage evidence.
checks.remediation: Make the canonical the same URL the sitemap lists; remove sitemap entries that robots.txt disallows.
checks.verification: For each sitemap URL, fetch it and assert the canonical equals the sitemap entry and robots.txt does not disallow it.

checks.title: The legal pages the jurisdiction requires exist and are linked
checks.why: SITUATIONAL because the requirement is jurisdictional, not universal: a German commercial site needs an Impressum, a US one does not. The skill reports what is missing for the declared region and does not assert a legal conclusion -- that is the domain-safety-disclaimer boundary, not this file's.
checks.remediation: Add the pages the declared region requires and link them from the footer of every page.
checks.verification: Assert each declared-required page returns 200 and is reachable from the home page in one click.

checks.title: Analytics fires only after consent, where consent is required
checks.why: Also jurisdictional, and the failure is asymmetric: analytics that never fires costs data, analytics that fires before consent costs a regulatory exposure.
checks.remediation: Gate the analytics snippet behind the consent state; do not load it on first paint.
checks.verification: Load the page with consent declined and assert no request to the analytics origin.

not_in_scope._comment: Named so a later contributor does not add them by analogy. Performance budgets and Lighthouse scoring are a different instrument with a different failure mode (a score is a gradient, these checks are binary), and `lighthouse` matching 0 files is NOT an argument for adding it here. Accessibility beyond alt text belongs to accessibility-auditor, which already exists and does it properly.

no_import_decision._comment: Step 0.3, recorded HERE rather than in the skill body, and the relocation is a correction the step needs rather than a liberty taken. 0.3 sits in Phase 0, whose Exit condition reads "zero skill code written" -- so its verify line ("the decision is written in the skill's own body") names an artefact its own phase forbids. The decision is what the step is about; it is recorded in the earliest durable place that exists, and the skill body restates it at 2.1 when there is a body.
no_import_decision.rule: The external corpus is a STUDY OBJECT and a per-defect harvest source. Its rule set is not imported. Rules enter ONE AT A TIME, each against a named defect, each carrying its own remediation and verification.
no_import_decision.why: An imported rule set arrives with its authors' assumptions about site type, jurisdiction and stack, and none of those is checked on arrival. The failure is silent: the skill grows to N checks, each individually plausible, and the conditional axis this file exists to enforce is the first thing a bulk import flattens. One-at-a-time keeps the axis honest because every entry has to answer `applies_to` before it lands.

regions._comment: Region axis (road-to-web-launch-readiness 2.3). Separate from site_types because it answers a different question: site_types decides WHETHER a check applies, regions decides HOW SEVERELY. A DE-targeted site owes Impressum and Datenschutz by law (TMG 5 / DSGVO Art. 13), so `required-legal-pages` is critical there and situational elsewhere -- the same check, a different tier. Modelled as a tier ESCALATION rather than as a second applies_to list, because a legal page is not more or less applicable in Germany, it is more or less optional.

escalations.why: TMG 5 obliges an Impressum and DSGVO Art. 13 a Datenschutzerklaerung for a DE-targeted commercial site. Abmahnung risk is real and immediate, which is what separates critical from situational here.
